newsitem.title: CANADA: FRACMASTER PRESIDENT QUELLS TAKEOVER TALK.
newsitem.headline: FRACMASTER PRESIDENT QUELLS TAKEOVER TALK.

text.p: Canadian Fracmaster Ltd President Les Margetak moved on Thursday to quell rumors that the Canadian oil services firm was set to be taken over.
Margetak took the unusual step of mentioning merger speculation in the company's second-quarter financial results press release.

"Recently I have been made aware of takeover or merger rumors regarding Canadian Fracmaster," he said. "While it is not our usual policy to comment on rumors, I would like to assure our employees that there are no discussions under way that involve the acquisition or merger of Canadian Fracmaster."
The company's stock price has risen since last October to all-time highs as North American oil services activity has boomed and Russia's oil industry climate has improved.

Fracmaster stock on the Toronto Stock Exchange late on Thursday was trading down 0.35 to 18.85 after rising as high as 19.35 earlier. It sank to 4.70 in late 1995 amid uncertainty over the Russian oil scene.
In Russia, Fracmaster takes oil in return for well stimulation services in various joint ventures and provides a growing number of fee-for-service well stimulation operations.

The company, buoyed by the abolishment of the country's oil export tariff and a narrowing of the domestic and export price gap, expects Russian operations to contribute C$25 million to 1997 earnings, up from C$20 million last year.
Margetak said at the company's annual meeting in May that Fracmaster was set to pump out earnings of C$1 a share in 1997, about double last year's result.
The company was still forecast to meet the target, Fracmaster chief financial officer Gary Sherkey told Reuters in a telephone interview on Thursday.
Fracmaster's improving performance had also led it over the past year to scrap plans for a reoraganization that could have included a spinoff of Russian operations.
Sherkey said Margetak's statement were placed in the release largely to squelch speculation among the company's employees.
"A whole bunch of our employees kept asking if our chairman was in negotiations. Well, we're not aware of any of that. We not...involved in any talks," he said.
Alfred Balm, the Geneva-based Fracmaster chairman and chief executive, owns about two-thirds of the company's stock.
"Right now, he supports us. He's not talking to anybody about selling this company, or we would have made that statement," Sherkey said.
He said the company's rising stock price was because of the rosy business fundamentals, not takeover speculation.
Fracmaster earlier reported second-quarter earnings of C$8 million or C19 cents a share, up 90 percent from the C$4.5 million or C10 cents a share posted in the same period last year.

Cash flow was C$17 million or C40 cents a share, up from C$16 million or C37 cents a share in the second quarter of 1996. Second-quarter revenues totalled C$98.6 million, up from C$80.3 million a year ago. ((Jeffrey Jones, Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
